correctness.rationale: The rank definition for finite simple graphs gives rk({v,w})>=1 iff all four adjacency profiles to an external x occur; unrolling empty and singleton extension quantifiers gives rk(X)>=3 iff some v has both a full adjacent partner a and full nonadjacent partner b. These jointly require at least three neighbors and at least three nonneighbors of v, so |V|>=7. They force six disjoint edge types: three incident v; an edge inside its neighbor set; a cross edge between neighbor and nonneighbor sets; an edge inside its nonneighbor set. At equality the profiles force the unique six-edge connected component {02,03,05,12,14,23} with all other vertices isolated, plus at least one isolate for (0,1) profile 00. Explicit v=0, adjacent a=2, nonadjacent b=1 has all four profiles in each pair. The component is asymmetric, so n!/(n-6)! labelled extremizers. Every universal graph containing all seven-vertex graphs contains the witness and has rank>=3, while disjoint union of every five-vertex graph type has no center with required three neighbors and two nonneighbors in one component, giving 6<=N(3)<=7. Distinguishes rank onset from universal forcing. Independent scratch enumeration confirmed no rank>=3 on 1..6 vertices and exactly 5040 six-edge seven-vertex graphs; the analytic argument extends all orders. Does not decide N(3)=6 vs7.

originality.rationale: The rank recursion is due to Kubiś–Shelah, with graph-rank framework and generic finite-rank witnesses in López-Callejas–Navarro-Castillo. Its full arXiv paper explicitly asks in Section 7 Question 7.4 for N(n) and states 4<=N(3)<=|H_3|, without the new six-edge unique extremizer or the 7-vertex onset. The target supplies a motivated sharp minimal graph classification and improves known bound to 6<=N(3)<=7. The exact remaining N(3) is explicitly unresolved; a graph atlas enumerates graphs but does not alone imply their one-point-extension ranks. Broader early rank literature not exhaustively checked.
